extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, IP attorneys, policymakers, and practitioners assessing prior art disclosure for novelty and inventive step
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and national practice for deciding whether and how a disclosure constitutes prior art for novelty and inventive step in patent examination and litigation, with special attention to new media (internet, email, intranets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of prior art disclosure on novelty & inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a prior disclosure prevents grant of a patent depends on novelty and inventive step standards. (Egypt) The application will be rejected upon examination for lack of novelty if it is the subject matter of any prior patent and/or pending patent application. The Egyptian Patent Office does not proceed with a thorough substantive examination thus there is no differentiation between assessment of novelty and inventive step. (Finland) Patents may be granted only for inventions which are new in relation to what was known before the filing date and which also differ 'essentially' therefrom; there are no differences between novelty and inventive step in this evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Country practice varies: some systems treat novelty and inventive step distinctly; others (or in some practice) use a single novelty-focused check. Note also how pending/published earlier applications may be treated differently for novelty vs inventive step (see separate metric).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory definition of prior art disclosure (Egypt Article 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 3 of Egyptian Patent Law: An invention shall not be considered new in two cases: (a) if the invention had really been publicly used in Egypt, or if its description or drawing had appeared in publications published in Egypt during the 50 years preceding the date of submission, provided the description/design is sufficiently clear to enable experts to exploit it; (b) if a patent had already been issued for the invention to another person or if an application had already been made for a patent by another person for the same invention or part thereof during the said 50-year period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a statutory (territorial + long-term) novelty bar: emphasizes publication/use in Egypt and a 50-year lookback. Draft laws may change this to absolute novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognised means/forms of disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: What counts as prior art: (Egypt) Mainly disclosure through written documents is recognised by law and practice; disclosure by use or oral disclosure must be corroborated with written evidence. (Finland) Everything made available to the public in writing, in lectures, by public use or otherwise shall be considered as prior art disclosure; all means of disclosure are recognised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must check national practice: some offices require corroborating evidence for non‑documentary disclosures; others treat all means equally. When relying on oral or use disclosures, obtain supporting contemporaneous written evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time limits for what counts as prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Temporal scope of prior art: (Egypt) Time of disclosure is limited to 50 years prior to the submission date (Article 3). (Finland) No limits as to time — absolute/objective novelty: all information available prior to filing is relevant. However, timing must be prior to the filing date for relevance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify national statute or draft law: timelines (e.g., long historical windows, six-month grace, or absolute novelty) materially change what references to search and cite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place/geographical relevance of disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the place of disclosure matters: (Egypt) Place of disclosure should be Egypt per Article 3, although internet publications available in Egypt are considered prior art; exhibitions recognized by law may be protected. (Finland) Place of disclosure is not relevant — disclosures anywhere in the world (in any language) may constitute a novelty bar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the national regime is territorial or global; check special clauses (exhibitions, treaties) that modify territoriality. For internet disclosures, assess accessibility in the jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhibition and evident-abuse exceptions / grace provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain disclosures do not destroy novelty: provisions for temporary protection if the invention was displayed at a recognized exhibition, and provisions allowing a patent despite an evident abuse disclosure or exhibition. (Danish/EPC-style 6-month rule referenced; Egyptian law provides temporary protection for official exhibitions; Finland allows recovery in case of evident abuse and exhibitions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for grace periods and exhibition exceptions: timing, recognized exhibitions list, and the evidentiary threshold for 'evident abuse' vary by jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of pending/unpublished applications
rubrics_metrics.description: How pending applications are treated as prior art: (Egypt) An application will be rejected for lack of novelty if the subject matter is the subject of any prior patent and/or pending patent application. (Finland) Published pending national, EPC (where Finland designated and fees paid), and international applications pursued in Finland are taken into account for novelty but not for inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between published and unpublished applications and between novelty vs inventive step effect; confirm whether national law recognises earlier-filed but later-published applications as prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal elements & confidentiality agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the identity/relationship of the discloser matter and are confidentiality agreements recognised? (Egypt) It makes no difference if disclosed by applicant or third party; the Patent Office will not recognise confidentiality agreements (this is a civil/contract matter). (Finland) In principle no differences regarding the person who discloses; confidentiality issues are handled in legal praxis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume a confidentiality agreement automatically prevents prior-art effect before checking whether national patent practice recognises it; confidentiality may be a contractual matter for courts rather than an administrative examiner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient ability / skilled-person understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirements about the recipient's ability to understand the disclosure: (Egypt) The ability of the public to understand the information is a criterion for assessing prior art disclosure. (Finland) Ability is appraised from the viewpoint of the person skilled in the art — the relevant question is how such a person would understand the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating whether a disclosure anticipates, frame the content as it would be understood by a person skilled in the art; this affects whether an allegedly-disclosing document is 'sufficiently clear to enable experts to exploit it.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverse engineering as a route to disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether reverse engineering can constitute disclosure: (Egypt) Reverse engineering is not mentioned in the current law; the Draft Patent Law would allow reverse engineering for scientific research only. (Finland) Possibility that a person might obtain the information through disassembly or reverse engineering can constitute a novelty bar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether publicly-available products, whose operation can be learned by reverse engineering, are treated as prior art in the relevant jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paperless / internet / new-media disclosures — sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether electronic/paperless information constitutes sufficient disclosure: Both groups state that internet/paperless information can be sufficient to affect novelty and inventive step. (Egypt) Internet publications that are available to the general public are rejected as prior art (chat/e-mail exceptions noted). (Finland) The medium is not limiting — all information available to the public by any means anywhere is relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat internet disclosures as potentially decisive prior art; but evaluate access restrictions, audience, and technical controls (see separate metrics). Obtain reliable timestamps and archived copies where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctions among online venues (intranets, extranets, WWW, chat, forums, email)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different network types may be treated differently: intranets/extranets with access controls are akin to private bulletin boards and may not be public; the Internet/WWW is generally open to public viewing; chat groups and forums are commonly regarded as public but depend on moderator/operator policy; emails may be private or public depending on recipients and distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess technical and administrative access controls, subscriber models, and the intended audience when treating online materials as prior art. Document how access was limited or open.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of encryption, passwords, and paid access on publicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Authentication, encryption and access control considerations: Encryption may be evidence of intent/confidentiality and render a disclosure non-public unless decoding tools are openly available. Passwords and payment requirements may affect whether a disclosure is public — if anyone may obtain a password (free or paid), the information may be considered publicly available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate how access is controlled: technically restricted access may rebut public availability, but paid/passworded access that is widely obtainable may still be public. Encryption interception and decryption by a third party may be treated as 'evident abuse' circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place of internet disclosure / accessibility test
rubrics_metrics.description: How to determine the place of disclosure for internet material: (Egypt) As long as the website is accessible to the general public in Egypt, it is considered a place of disclosure. (Finland) Geographical place is irrelevant and mere possibility of access is sufficient; information made available via the Internet may be considered available worldwide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the website was accessible in the jurisdiction and whether access was realistic for the skilled person. For cross-border cases, check whether national law treats internet availability as global or territorial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing, duration of availability, and archives for internet disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirements for timing/duration: (Egypt) No specific requirements for timing or duration of internet information; archives are not necessary. (Finland) Timing must be prior to filing; duration of availability is in principle not relevant though a very short period may render the disclosure non-public if no chance to view existed; archives are useful evidence but their value depends on provider reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, secure archived snapshots (e.g., web-archives, third-party timestamps) to prove content and timing. Consider the practical availability to the public, not merely technical uptime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and standard of proof for internet and other disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Who must prove a disclosure and what standards apply: (Egypt) In court cases one must provide a written document as evidence of prior art disclosure and there are no specific rules for internet evidence. (Finland) A party claiming a disclosure has occurred should carry the burden of proof; evidence principles should remain technology-neutral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When alleging an internet disclosure, be prepared to show contemporaneous, reliable evidence (archived pages, timestamps, logs). Courts may be skeptical of unaudited digital evidence because of ease of manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidential value and risk of manipulation of digital information
rubrics_metrics.description: Digital information is easy to modify; manipulation potential affects evidential value. There are currently no specific rules governing digital-manipulation risk, but examiners/courts should be aware of technical nuances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use trusted third-party archival/verification services, cryptographic timestamps, or neutral repositories to improve evidentiary weight. The Finnish Group suggested creating praxis or third-party services to store/verify Internet disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy/harmonisation considerations (EPC/TRIPS and draft laws)
rubrics_metrics.description: Several groups favour harmonisation with EPC/TRIPS standards. Draft laws (e.g., Egyptian Draft Patent Act) may shift from relative (territorial/long-term) novelty to absolute novelty and may extend protection to utility models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor legislative reform and international harmonisation efforts which may change thresholds for novelty, the treatment of new media, and the protection term for utility models.
